Useful String Methods

Stage 4 Demo ⏱ 14 min 📖 Glossary

Strings ship with a power toolkit: measure, peek, slice, find, compare, clean, split. Seven methods handle roughly 90% of all text work you will ever do.

🔎 Motivating questionIf books had instant tools — ruler, tweezers, scissors, finder — which would you reach for daily?

Objectives

  • Use length, charAt, substring
  • Compare with equals
  • Split and trim text

Needs first: Two-Dimensional Arrays

1 Start with an analogy

Real life first, code second.

The Swiss knife. length() the ruler, charAt() the tweezers, substring() the scissors, equals() the scale, toUpperCase() the megaphone, trim() the towel, split() the cutter. One tool per job.

⚠️ Where the analogy breaksWhere it breaks: real scissors cut the original. String scissors return FRESH paper — the original never changes (immutability, next lesson). Forgetting this discards every “edit”.

2 The concept, plainly

One idea at a time, words before jargon.

Measure & peek: length(), charAt(i) (0-based, crashes past the end like arrays), indexOf(x) returning −1 for “absent”.

Slice: substring(start, end) — start INCLUDED, end EXCLUDED. "Java".substring(0, 2) is "Ja", never "Jav".

Compare & clean: equals() and equalsIgnoreCase() for content; toUpperCase()/toLowerCase(); trim() shaves edge whitespace; split(",") cuts "a,b" into ["a","b"].

Case matters everywhere: equals is exact, indexOf finds exact case, and charAt(length) is out-of-bounds — text has doors too.

⚙️ Tech details — precise facts
  • substring shares nothing (modern JVMs copy) — but treat results as fresh strings regardless; the original is never modified.
  • split takes a REGEX, not plain text: split(".") splits on EVERYTHING (dot = any char). Escape it: split("\\."). A genuine trap.
  • indexOf has overloads: indexOf("a", 5) searches FROM position 5 — the backbone of find-all loops.

3 Watch it move: Swiss knife demo

Step at your pace. Text explains every move.

4 Live code demo

Small, correct Java 17 (LTS) code. Read, trace, copy.

Main.javaJava 17
public class Main {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    String s = "  Java Rocks  ";
    String clean = s.trim();
    System.out.println(clean);
    System.out.println("len = " + clean.length());
    System.out.println("Java vs java: " + "Java".equals("java"));
    System.out.println("slice = " + "Java".substring(0, 2));
    System.out.println("at = " + "Java".indexOf("v"));
  }
}
▶ Output Java Rocks len = 10 Java vs java: false slice = Ja at = 2
  • trim shaves edge spaces → "Java Rocks", length 10.
  • equals is case-exact → false.
  • substring(0,2) keeps 0–1 → "Ja"; indexOf("v") → 2.
▶️ Run it yourselfSave exactly as Main.java, then javac Main.java and java Main. Every full program in this course works this way.
💡 Why this output?Cleaned, measured, compared (case counts!), sliced with excluded end, located by position.

6 Common mistakes (at least 3)

Wrong, why, fixed — learn from realistic slips.

❌ Mistake 1: s == "Java" to compare words.Why: Identity again — same content, usually different houses.
✅ Fix: s.equals("Java") for content, always.
❌ Mistake 2: substring(0, 5) expecting FIVE inclusive chars.Why: End index is EXCLUDED: 0..5 yields positions 0–4.
✅ Fix: Want 5 chars? substring(0, 5) gives exactly 5 — positions 0,1,2,3,4.
❌ Mistake 3: s.trim(); then using s unchanged.Why: trim returns a FRESH string; the call alone edits nothing.
✅ Fix: Catch it: s = s.trim();
❌ Mistake 4: split(".") to cut on dots.Why: split takes REGEX — "." means “any character”, shredding everything.
✅ Fix: Escape it: split("\\.") — regex tax.

7 Guided practice

Hints first, solutions only after a real try.

First three

Take the first 3 characters of any name variable.

Hintsubstring(0, 3).
Solutionname.substring(0, 3); // positions 0,1,2
Find the @

Check whether an email String contains "@".

HintindexOf returns −1 when absent.
Solutionemail.indexOf("@") != -1;

9 Takeaways + next step

  • Seven tools cover nearly all text jobs.
  • End index excluded; −1 means absent.
  • Methods return fresh strings — catch them.
  • Case always matters; split takes regex.
